title: Caring for the sick
hookLine: care as seva, with rest for the carer
tomorrow: Simran's been 'fine' all week. she isn't. who does she tell?

lines: A DAD ASLEEP IN A CHAIR.
cards: Hospital coffee from the machine by the elevator tastes mostly like the paper cup. Harjit has been drinking it for four days.
He's slept in the vinyl chair beside Bebe's bed every night, still in his work jacket, phone on his chest in case the dispatcher calls. On the fifth evening Simran walks in with a thermos.
She unscrews the lid and the room fills with cardamom and ginger, Bebe's kind of chai. Harjit looks up, and for a second he looks like he might cry.

teach.h: TARN TARAN: CARE FOR THE SHUNNED.
teach.b: Caring for the sick is seva. Tradition says Guru Arjan, at Tarn Taran, set up a place of care for people with leprosy, people others kept away from, and served them there.

In the Sukhmani, on Ang 286, he says, in paraphrase: whoever does seva without wanting anything back reaches the Master. That's what Harjit is doing in the vinyl chair. But look at the same line from the other side.

teach.h: A SEVADAR IS A PERSON TOO.
teach.b: A sevadar is a person too. Seva with no wage still costs sleep, meals, a back that aches from the chair.

teach.h: SHIFTS, DAL, A RIDE ON THURSDAYS.
teach.b: In a sangat, nobody is meant to carry it alone, which is why langar has shifts and why kirtan has more than one singer.
So caring for the sick has two halves: the care, and the care of whoever is giving it. Simran takes the night shift. Two aunties from the gurdwara drop off dal and rotis at the house.
Maya's mom texts that she can drive Bebe to physical therapy on Thursdays. Harjit goes home and sleeps in a bed. In the morning he comes back shaved, and the chai is still warm in the thermos.

how: When someone in a Sikh family is ill, relatives and the sangat take turns at the bedside, bring cooked food, run errands, and include the sick and their carers in Ardas.

games.q: what does “caring for the sick” mean?
o: a nurse's job that families should stay out of
seva at the bedside, shared so the carer can rest
praying for the sick from a distance only

games.q: caring for the sick — tap the pairs.
p: one who serves, and a person too
so Harjit can sleep in a bed

s: a good sevadar should carry the care alone, without rest
a sevadar is a person too; in a sangat, nobody is meant to carry it alone.
tradition says Guru Arjan served people with leprosy at Tarn Taran
people others kept away from were cared for there.
seva at a bedside counts less than seva at the gurdwara
caring for the sick is seva, as Guru Arjan showed at Tarn Taran.

games.q: a friend has cared for her sick mom every night for two weeks and says, 'i'm fine, it's my seva.' what fits today?
o: it is seva, and you need care too. let me take Tuesday.
you're right; real seva means never asking for a break.
you should hire someone so it stops being your problem.
games.why: Ang 286 honors seva that wants nothing back, and a sangat shares the load so the carer can rest. both halves are the care.

practice: Make or pour something warm to drink, and hold the cup close before you sip. Breathe in its smell slowly for the whole sit, the way Harjit breathed in that chai.
Let it be a small care for the one doing the caring, even if that's you.

wordCard.voice: Caring for the sick. Seva at the bedside, given freely, with others stepping in so the carer can rest.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sevadar, one who does seva, at the gurdwara or at a bedside.

carryVoice: Something to keep: care for the carers, a thermos and a night shift. Day 1719, warm.

sources.ref: Ang 286, Sukhmani 18, Guru Arjan (sevaa karat hoe nihkaamee, tis kau hot paraapat suaamee), paraphrased
